utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If I could remind you, Colonel Doyle, of the affirmation which you took yesterday which still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Doyle, can you tell me who Vera Ljubovic is, what kind of contact you have with her, and why she provides you with information.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vera Ljubovic was provided by the authorities in Bosnia to assist the mission, and she did that by making herself available, when she was requested, for translations and as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Vera Ljubovic on the premises where the mission's offices were or was she at the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was at the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina for most of the time. She was at the mission when she was requested to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean then, in view of the fact that she drew your attention to the articles from the Oslobodjenje daily, that you were perhaps criticised for the statements made in relation to your visit to Trebinje, that is to say criticised by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall at any stage in the 12 months that I was in Bosnia that there was criticism levelled at my performance or anything that I had done, so I don't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the meeting in Trebinje, did General Strugar perhaps mention to you that he had to go to Belgrade on that day?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no, and he didn't say it to me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know Admiral Jokic. I don't recall whether I had met him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just before giving evidence here yesterday, you read a note that was made last year when you talked to the Prosecution team; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you indicate to the Prosecution then that some corrections had to be made in those notes?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did this on the 3rd of February, 2004, on the day you gave evidence, that that is when you made the corrections?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to place the correction on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, can you just read this sentence, the one that is a correction of the sentence you gave in your previous statement.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the notes of the interview with Colonel Colm Doyle dated the 30th of July, 2003, in paragraph 10 the second sentence should be corrected to read as follows: 'What he meant was that it was revenge as a result of casualties General Strugar had received from unspecified paramilitaries.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that although you read the contents just before giving evidence, that is to say the contents of the notes dated the 30th of July, 2003, you did not answer my question as to when you had that meeting with the Prosecution? Yesterday you said that this meeting took place with the Prosecution towards the end of August, and according to paragraph 4 of the notes, the meeting was held on the 30th of July at 6:00 p.m. in the Tribunal building.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been to the Tribunal on five occasions. I can't remember exact dates as to -- I know the approximate dates but I don't know them exactly. I can't recall them without reading them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Just before entering the courtroom yesterday, you read the notes dated the 30th of July last year, and you made a correction with regard to that note. And you said to me that you had this meeting towards the end of August and that it took place sometime during the day, late in the morning. Isn't that right? Could you please give me a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to assist here. I was here at the Tribunal in July and I was here at the Tribunal in August. I wasn't too sure which of those occasions it was that I made that statement. I didn't read the date of the statement, I just read the content of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 in these notes, the date and the time when you provided the statement is given. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that specifically. I know generally what I -- the statement I had made. I don't know every single word without reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that you do not remember what you did six months ago when this meeting was held and when the notes were made?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know in general what I did six months ago when the meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not remember important information from the notes that you read just before giving testimony?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that you did not give a statement to the investigators in 1996, as you repeated several times yesterday, but this, rather, took place in 1995? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that you confirmed several times in relation to your meeting with General Strugar that you know that he was commander of the 2nd Operative Group?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I said that he was the commander of the 2nd Operative Group, I don't think the word "Operative" is correct. He was the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. When I met with General Strugar, it was my impression, or I had been informed or I assumed that he was the commander of the 2nd Corps group. The word "Operational Group" is not in the normal chain of military formations. Several corps are normally called divisions. So this was not a phrase that I was totally familiar with until later. I'm not too sure when I realised it was the 2nd Operational Group, but for the period that I was in Bosnia, I had thought it was the 2nd Corps group. That's what I wrote on the back of that photograph. To me, it wasn't a significant -- it wasn't a significant issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that in spite of that, that is not the way you put it to the investigators in your statement? You told them several times that General Strugar was commander of the 4th Military District. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall -- I don't recall stating that it was the 4th Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher for his assistance, please, to have this document distributed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would object to the misleading nature of the question. I'm sure as the Chamber peruses the statement, there are not multiple references. It is simply incorrect. It is a 16-page -- 17-page statement, and if the Chamber peruses it, the thrust of it is about the role in Bosnia. There is one paragraph on page 6 which mentions, as a peripheral issue in the context of an investigation for the events in Bosnia and Sarajevo, Strugar, and I -- and the reference of one time is -- reference to the commander of the 4th Military District is a one-time reference. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I propose to wait until we learn what it is that Mr. Rodic wants to make of the statement before forming any view on that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, in the second paragraph -- in the second line of paragraph 34, you say he was commander of the 4th Military District; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I see in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please take a look - and now I'm saying this for Ms. Somers' benefit - look at page 5, paragraph 23. The one but last sentence: "The 4th Military District was in Trebinje. It consisted of Trebinje itself." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that extract. Can you direct me to the page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 23 on page 5, the one but last sentence. "The 4th Military District was in Trebinje, and it encompassed Trebinje itself, the 13th Corps in Bileca, and the 37th Corps in Nevesinje." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I have in the statement, yes. That's what I believed it to be at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that you stated to the investigators in this same statement several times that General Strugar was commander of the 4th Military District and that the 4th Military District was in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's what is in the statement, that's what I believed it to be. There seems to be very little doubt that General Strugar was in command of whatever formation was down in Trebinje. That's not in dispute. The title of the unit may well be and I accept that I was wrong on that occasion. It has since been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also correct that soon after the meeting -- soon after the meeting on the 6th of December you wrote down that General Strugar was commander of the 2nd Corps group, and you never stated that to anyone again after that? This is what was on the back of the photograph; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what was written on the photograph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that already in Oslobodjenje, dated the 8th of December, in the translation of the text that Vera Ljubovic sent to you, reference is made to General Strugar as commander of the Operations Group? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it does state that he was the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, not Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also correct that the first time you said that General Strugar was commander of the 2nd Operational Group only in the year 2000, on the 23rd of August, and that this was done at the suggestion made by the Prosecution? This has to do with what you wrote in hand underneath the picture.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that may be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that General Strugar made a reference to a number of casualties related to the 6th of December, 1991? That is not correct; right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- sorry, could you ask that question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that General Strugar did not give you information about 16 casualties, 16 persons who were killed, and that is what you wrote on the back of the photograph on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall General Strugar mentioning any numbers to me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is also correct that you do not recall where you did get this information from.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is correct what you said yesterday, that you do not recall whether you watched the TV reports about Dubrovnik, dated the 6th of December, and whether you made an entry in your diary after that. And I quote: "Bad in Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is correct that in paragraph 34, on page 6 of your statement given to the Prosecution in 1995, in the last sentence of that paragraph, you say: "That night, on television I saw reports on the shelling of Dubrovnik, that Dubrovnik had been shelled." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that in the -- in paragraph 10 of the notes dated the 30th of July, 2003, that you know nothing about the damages sustained by Dubrovnik since you never went to the city itself, but that you had the impression that the actual damages were less than what the Croats had depicted -- had, rather, shown, and you did not take for granted everything that the Croats said because they were prone to resort to propaganda? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in paragraph 13 of the same notes you said that you did not know anything about any persons who were killed or about the units that took part in the campaign?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not know what General Strugar's rank was? You believed that he was a three-star general because other people had told you that he had three stars. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that General Strugar held the rank of general. How many stars he had, I wasn't totally sure. I accepted what I was told, which was that he was a three-star.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You accepted and said yesterday that he was a lieutenant general with three stars and that that is what others had explained to you. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then it is correct also that you did not see General Strugar's rank insignia at all. Rather, you did not see three stars on his uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall what rank I saw on General Strugar's uniform. It may have been three stars. I just don't remember. It is now 13 years since I met him, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you. Yesterday you said that you were told in relation to General Strugar that he held the rank of lieutenant general, which corresponds to a three-star general, insignia involving three stars, and you never mentioned the possibility of having seen anything that could have resembled three stars on his uniform. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to -- I'm trying to get to understand what exactly -- can you please -- can you please repeat that again? I don't fully understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that upon your arrival in Trebinje, you were told that Pavle Strugar is a lieutenant general and that that rank involves three stars. Also, you said yesterday that you yourself did not see three stars but that you wrote this in your diary because you accepted that he was a lieutenant general because you had been told that he had three stars, that he was a three-star general. Is that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said yesterday. I should point out that in some armies it's not necessarily that a general would have three stars. He may have had different sort of -- some people have various insignia indicating their rank. My assumption is that a three-star general is somebody who wears three stars. I do not know, and I cannot recall what the format of that is on the uniform of a JNA officer. I was introduced -- or General Strugar was introduced to me as Lieutenant General Strugar. I accepted him as a lieutenant general, and that has never been in issue since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is true and correct that for the first time on the 30th of July of last year you said in a note that you saw General Strugar again in February 1992 in Bileca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also right that in paragraph 12 of last year's note that you said that when you met him then you didn't notice that his rank had been put down one rung?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you cannot actually know that fact because you had no personal knowledge of it in the sense of you knowing about it and you seeing rank insignia on General Strugar's uniform which would denote in his rank in any way? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that in your statement to the investigators in 1995, in paragraph 34 you said that General -- or, rather, Strugar was a lieutenant general and that you never mentioned the number of stars in relation to his rank?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to him as a lieutenant general because I was told he was a lieutenant general. How long he was a lieutenant general for I don't know, how many stars he had on his uniform I don't know. I just know him -- or I was introduced to him as lieutenant general, and that's what I referred to him since then as.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, when was he introduced to you as being lieutenant general?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume it was done when I met him first on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I'm not getting the interpretation. You just confirmed a moment ago that it was true and correct that you were -- that he was introduced to you as lieutenant general in 1991, isn't that right, and not as colonel general?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not too sure where the rank colonel general has come from. I understood that General Strugar held the rank of lieutenant general, and I haven't changed that at any stage. I don't recall ever coming across or having a reference to the rank of colonel general. I don't understand that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But nonetheless, in your statement, the first one that you gave to the investigators, it said that he was colonel general. That's what it says in the statement; is that right? Paragraph 34, second sentence -- or rather, the first sentence, I apologise. It says: "That same day before meeting the mayor, I met --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel says "colonel general," "pukovnik," rather than "potpukovnik," "lieutenant general."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I point out, Mr. Rodic, that in the English version which we have, it shows "lieutenant general."

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Then I'm reading from -- Your Honour, I'm reading the translation in Serbian. I do apologise if in the English version it does indeed say "lieutenant general." I apologise. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that in the first sentence of paragraph 7 of the note from last year, that you say that General Strugar told the members of the observer mission, monitoring mission, that he wasn't in a good mood?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And then in the third sentence of that same paragraph, paragraph number 7 of the note, you say the following, that he was angry while he was speaking, while he was saying that he had to resort to opening fire at Dubrovnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also right that in sentence four of that same paragraph, number 7 of your note, that you said that you gained the impression that the general's conduct was motivated by the desire to punish? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm looking --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We do not have the actual text.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: It is the passage or, rather, paragraph 7. The last sentence in that paragraph. "General Strugar acknowledged that he issued the orders for the action and Colonel Doyle gained the impression that under these conditions the conduct of General Strugar was motivated with a desire to retaliate or punish." And that is paragraph 7 of your note. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading the note here and it states that his action had been punitive, which was an indication that the action had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it also true that in the second sentence of paragraph 8, on page 2 of your note, you said that you gained the impression that the order was that sporadic fire at random should be opened on Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise that we do not have the document so we can't read the actual words.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the second sentence of paragraph 8 of your note of last year, that you said that you had the impression that the order was that random fire should be opened at Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I object and just ask, to simplify it for the interpreters, that the witness simply read what's being asked of him. It's in front of him and it might make less of a mess for the poor interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The sentence being put to the witness is in paragraph 7, document page 03340133, and it reads in the English version: "General Strugar had admitted to having given the order for attack, and it was Colonel Doyle's impression that, in the circumstances, General Strugar's course of action had been punitive." And then the next passage put to the witness was in paragraph 8 of the same page, the second sentence: "Moreover, General Strugar did not inform the witness of the targets (or the type of targets) being engaged in Dubrovnik on that day, and it was Colonel Doyle's impression that the firing on Dubrovnik had been ordered indiscriminately." I think they're the sentences you are putting to the witness, are they, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, is it true that that is indeed what you stated?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that in paragraph 9 of that same note that you said that General Strugar was very angry during the talks?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was very angry while speaking. And in paragraph 10, you explain that General Strugar, when talking about resorting to firing, that he meant that it was revenge as a result of casualties suffered by his own units. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was my impression that the general had resorted to firing on Dubrovnik because he wasn't prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be sufficient in view of the time we have at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We ask that if the witness is asked a question and he starts to answer, he be allowed to complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had the impression the witness had finished. Was there anything more, Colonel, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm satisfied with the statement that I have in front of me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm doing my best that in asking my questions to give the witness the number of the paragraph in which the sentence is contained, and he has the statement before him to be able to find his way around it. Mr. Doyle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only problem, Mr. Rodic, is the written transcript doesn't always reveal what's there and what it is the witness is being asked about, but if there is confusion, I will interrupt to make that more clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, is it also correct, Mr. Doyle, that opposed to all your previous impressions, the ones we have just stated and shown through your questions and the impressions you gained first of all, in paragraph 34 of your statement given in 1995, you said only that the general was irritated over the matters he described as having taken place in Dubrovnik? Is that correct? And it is sentence three in paragraph 34. "Annoyance" is the word. The general expressed his annoyance at what he expressed was happening in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: May we agree, Mr. Doyle, that it is also correct that based on your impressions as expressed in the note itself of 2003, that there is nothing either in your diary of the 6th of December, 1991, that there is nothing of this in your diary?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: My diary reflects the fact that I met General Strugar and the time -- the approximate time I met him at. There's nothing in my diary which talks about impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that for the first time yesterday, in fact, you said that General Strugar was courteous to you and that you gained the impression that he was thinking about other things, that he had other things on his mind during the meeting? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also correct that you said yesterday that the translator informed you that General Strugar was angry at the paramilitaries because they had attacked his units? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also right that in paragraph 7 of the note dated back to last year that you said that at the beginning of the meeting, General Strugar said that he was not in a good mood because his troops had suffered casualties? And that's the first sentence. His troops had suffered losses.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that in that same paragraph you said that you assumed that the paramilitary units from -- attacked federal army units on the territory of Bosnia, or from the territory of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my assumption, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Doyle, it is also correct that in your 1995 statement, when you talked to the representatives of the OTP for the first time, in paragraph 34, make no mention of the fact that the general was angry at the paramilitary formations or that his units had suffered losses as a result of the paramilitaries' actions; is that true?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but the paragraph did mention that the general was expressing his annoyance.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference between anger and annoyance and annoyance and extremely angry? What were your impressions as to the terms you used in what you said last year? Would you say there was a difference between the terms?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a significant difference, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although in your statement of 1995, you said that General Strugar told you that on that day he had shelled Dubrovnik, in the 2003 note that he acknowledged having issued an order that fired the open -- to open fire on Dubrovnik, is it true that you did not record that in your diary at the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't record that in my diary in 1991, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you did not file a report to your mission about that fact, informing them of that event?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that you did not do that, that is to say write the report or inform anybody although you were considerably surprised by the fact that a general should acknowledge something like that? And you said that that had never happened before in your entire career. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Usually acknowledgements of that kind by a general would be recorded on film, by camera, but you did nothing to record the sentence at all in any way. That would be true, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: However, it is also true that in paragraph 10 of the note you say -- or, rather, that your statement was, and would you have a look at it, please, it is the first sentence: "Although I do not remember the actual words, it was his impression that General Strugar was talking in general terms about opening fire, not in specific terms." Did you say words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, may we agree then that in my previous questions I put to you your statements from 1995 and from your note in 2003 as well as what you said yesterday during your testimony, as well as the documents that have become exhibits in this case? Is that correct? Did I do that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have referred to all of the documents in the course of your questioning of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Apart from the documents, did I also put your own statements back to you, what you said during yesterday's examination, what you told the investigators in 1995, and the note given or compiled on the 30th of July last year? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm getting a little bit confused by the manner in which you are -- you're making reference here. Anything -- any question you've asked me, I've answered, and that's all I'm saying. I'm referring to the documents that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Mr. Doyle, that you have answered my questions, but what I actually meant, and the substance of my own question was this: May we agree that I, through my previous questions from the beginning of today's day, I quoted your actual statements, what you told the investigators in your statement in 1995, then I put your own note to you dated the 30th of July, 2003, and also I referred to the examination conducted here yesterday. So do you agree that I put your own statements to you taken from those documents and from yesterday's testimony? Would that be correct? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a simple question on a very long statement. All I can say is that I'm answering the questions truthfully. You are referring to these documents, and you're asking me specific questions which I'm answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Your 1995 statement is a long one, and do you agree with me when I say that most of it refers to -- most of the questions referred to paragraph 34 of that same statement and the sentences that were quoted were contained in that paragraph? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that through my questions I also indicated individual quotations from 14 paragraphs, which is your July 2003 statement? That's what it's composed of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quoting from both of those statements. I'm not sure how many individual quotations you are quoting, but I accept that you are dealing with issues that were -- appeared in the statement of 1995 and the statement I made in '03.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that I also asked you about what your responses were yesterday to the questions asked during the examination? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've asked me questions about the statement and what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, may we agree, then, that in certain passages that I quoted from your statements there are a number of differences, discrepancies? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't accept that there are many discrepancies. There are differences in words and there are differences in interpretations, but I don't -- I don't believe there are many discrepancies. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, is it true and correct that three words from your diary, and I quote them, "bad in Dubrovnik," and you reported those upon returning to Sarajevo, are the only written evidence and traces of your meeting with General Strugar? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are the only words written in the diary apart from the words "1200 hours, met with General Strugar," and the reference that he was a three-star or a lieutenant general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Doyle. Now, is it true and correct that everything you said in your statement dated 1995, except for the fact about a meeting held with General Strugar, is not recorded anywhere else, not even in your own diary? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The statement of 1995 was an accurate reflection of everything I was asked or happened to me in the year I spent in Yugoslavia. That detail is not contained in any diary because it wasn't meant to be contained in a diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's clarify that point, Mr. Doyle. Eight sentences in paragraph 34 of your statement given to the investigators, except the fact that in those eight lines you had a meeting with General Strugar, which can be seen also from excerpts in your diary of the 6th of December, 1991, nothing further from that paragraph has been recorded either in your diary or anywhere else; is that right? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that a lengthy note on your statement from 2003 is an expanded edition of paragraph 34 dated 1995?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the note you mention certain things, certain facts, impressions, and so on of which there is not a single word in the 1995 statement?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement I made in '03 is a -- a more comprehensive statement in relation to the general content of the paragraph 34 in my statement of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When I asked you at the beginning of the day today about the fact that just prior to your testimony here you read the note through and that you weren't able to tell me exactly when you actually conducted that conversation with the OTP, at what time and what date, I gained the impression that although you read through this prior to your testimony, you now, after a lot of time has gone by from the meeting that you had in 1991 with General Strugar, that you're now expanding on your statement, and you're telling us a longer story by including facts, impressions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was that, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is comment by the Defence, which is argument, which is saved for a later point in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's being put as a question for the witness to react to. I will allow the question. Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me put it in simpler terms, Mr. Doyle. May we agree that there is a noticeable difference in gradation with respect to what you recorded in your diary on the 6th of December, 1991, up to what you said in your 2003 note? Can we agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree when -- if you say that the note of the statement of '03 is an expansion of the general content of paragraph 34 of the statement I made in 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we also agree that all of this is a general expansion in reference to two sentences from the diary from the 6th of December, 1991, and these two sentences read: "Meeting with General Strugar in Dubrovnik. Bad in Dubrovnik." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the entry in my diary of the 6th of December, 1991, was not done in any way to give an explanation of the content of my meeting with General Strugar. The content in the diary is a record of who I met or the fact that I met with General Strugar at approximately 1200 hours on the 6th of December, 1991, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I fully understand you, Mr. Doyle, but I cannot refer to anything else but that diary, because you said yourself that you did not write any kind of report in relation to that meeting. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that your observations, impressions, new facts are becoming increasingly expressed the more time goes by? For example, you seem to remember more 13 years later than four years later. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we cannot agree on that. I do not remember 13 years later what I may have remembered in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But your notes from 2003 corroborate what I said just now, because it is much longer than that eight-line paragraph from the interview you had with the investigators in 1995, and it challenges quite a bit of that. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that it challenges. The statement I made in 1995 was a witness statement of a full and very busy 12 months I spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The statement of '03 is a more detailed statement of the one meeting that I had on the 6th of December with General Strugar and my impressions of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you interpret exactly now here before this Court what General Strugar had said to you actually? Do you remember that now? The exact sentences that he said, can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember the exact sentences, word by word, of what General Strugar said through his interpreter. I know the general content and impressions from that time. Yes, I can relate to those. But exactly what he said I'm not in a position to say. Word-for-word, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, can we agree that there cannot be two, three, or several truths?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving -- I'm giving -- I'm answering these the best way I can. It's not a question of untruths. That would give an indication to me that I'm giving untruths, which I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, I am saying that for reasons known only to you, you mentioned many things that were simply speculation during your statement here, and many untruths in relation to General Strugar. I have pointed out to you significant differences in all the evidence you have given.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to tender the statement from 1995 and the note from 2003 to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just before you do, Mr. Rodic, you put what I assumed was a question to the witness just then, although it was framed unclearly whether it was a statement or a question. I wonder whether the colonel would like to answer that question. You put to him that he's mentioned many things that were simply speculation, and many untruths, and these were evident from the differences in all that he'd said. Is that something that you accept, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I do not accept it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Rodic, we have given you very -- almost extreme liberty in this cross-examination, both as to length and as to content, because the Chamber has been conscious that this witness is of considerable importance to your case, but I think you can take it that we well and truly appreciate that there were recorded in 1991 very few words, that a longer statement was made which contains much more detail in 1995, and that the statement in 2003 contains material that was not recorded earlier. We appreciate all of that, and we appreciate that you questioned the reliability and I think the honesty of what is put in 2003 and now, and we've gained a very clear impression of that from your cross-examination. So you now wish to tender both of the two statements that were put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your understanding in relation to the length of time allocated to me for the cross-examination in view of the importance of the subject matter involved, as you said. I would just like to tender these statements or, rather, the statement and the notes into evidence on behalf of the Defence, and I just have a few more questions left that I would like to put to the witness, a few brief questions. And then I would like to ask you to rule on these matters that I shall refer to subsequently, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it the basis upon which you tender these two statements is that the content of them has been most material to the cross-examination that you have made and material matters upon which the Defence relies contained in these two statements have been accepted by the witness as matters that he stated in 1995 and 2003. Is there any objection, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: My response, Your Honour, is, as has been discussed before, is the practice that clearly these are not evidence. I'm hopeful that we will not go -- undertake a pattern of using this. This is not a civil system. If it will assist the Chamber, then on that basis and restricted on that basis, I would indicate that the objection would only be limited as to the practice, but in this instance it would make -- if it's helpful, then we would agree to that. I would also ask the Chamber please take note that there was a correction made by the witness and it would be helpful if Mr. Rodic would provide a copy of the paragraph in the note of, I believe, July of '03 so that the Chamber has that as part as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Somers. Can I indicate that we fully agree that it is not appropriate and that it should not be normal that witness statements come into evidence in this way. In the case of this particular witness, there have been detailed and material passages of some length. The precise differences between them are -- have been relied on by Mr. Rodic and will be relied on in the Defence. While they can probably be gleaned from the record, as you yourself did indicate in your objection which I haven't lost sight of but which I thought took care of itself as time went on, there may not be entire clarity at times as to precisely what the statement contained. It would appear useful on this occasion and for that reason that the Chamber have the precise and accurate statements both of 1995 and 2003. And I agree entirely with you with the correcting note made this month by the witness. I don't believe the Chamber has a copy of that correcting note yet, Mr. Rodic. Do you have one?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have one copy, but during the break I'll photocopy it and then the copy can be admitted into evidence and I'll hand it over to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, I notice the statement of 1995, which I accept from the evidence of the colonel as a statement that he agrees he made, in the form that has been placed before us omits paragraphs 84 to 96. It does appear that it includes all the numbered pages that have been given a document number, but if you notice, between page 03340034 and 03340035, there appear to be omitted some pages of the original document, and they would appear to include paragraphs 84 to 96. They are not paragraphs to which any reference has been made in the course of the evidence, so we can receive the document in this form, but I draw attention to that omission in case either party thinks it may be material.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I call to Your Honours' attention, and I believe yesterday you might have gleaned this as well, the version of the statement to which I was referring is not the one that was used in a 92 bis format, which has actual paragraphing. It might be more helpful just to have the complete 1995 statement, which bears an ERN of 00332172 et seq., and that goes on for 18 pages with 2189 as the final page. I would leave it to the Chamber's discretion, but that is the 1995 signed version.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We gave you the statements that were disclosed to us. This is the form that we received them in. We have two such statements in English that have those two paragraphs missing, as you noted yourself. But in the statement in the Serbian language, we realised that these paragraphs are not relevant to General Strugar's case, and we did not refer to them at all during our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Rodic. We will receive the documents in the form that they've been given to us by you, and there will be a third document, which will be the February 2004 further correction by the witness, which will be added during the break, as soon as it is available. So if the court officer would give these their exhibit number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement of the witness from 1995 will be Defence Exhibit D20; the notes of the interview of the witness Defence Exhibit D21; and the correcting note of the 3rd of February, 2004, will be Defence Exhibit D22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Rodic --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I just put two or three more questions, very brief ones, and then I would like to put forward my proposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Doyle, can you tell me this: The text that you wrote and that you explained in relation to the photograph, the 6th of December, 1991, and this text that you wrote on the 23rd of August, 2003, could you please tell me where this was written. Was it written on a separate piece of paper or on a document, or did you perhaps write this on the back of this photograph? Can you tell us a bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I wrote that on a -- on a document or on a blank sheet of paper that was attached to the photograph to indicate who was in the photograph, the one that I have dated that you have in your hand there. I do not believe I wrote -- in fact, I'm -- I'm almost sure I did not write that actually on the photograph itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether, in addition to the excerpts from your diary that you gave us here, did you record anything in 1992, meetings and facts that were important to you, and inter alia, the fact that in February 1992 you met General Strugar again?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me did -- did I record anything in 1992. Do you mean 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I mean did you keep the same diary in 1992? Also, in February 1992, if you kept such a diary, did you record that you met General Strugar yet again? And also, did you refer to other meetings in your diary if you still kept it?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my practice to record in my diary, both in 1991 and 1992, the personalities that I would have met. I did not record the content of any major discussion I had in those diaries, but, yes, the diary of 1992 would -- I cannot be certain, but I would assume that the record of the ambassador who was head of the monitor mission, Ambassador Salgueiro and his officials, when we met with General Strugar in February of 1992, I assume that I probably would have put that fact into my diary of 1992. I don't have it in front of me so I'm not too sure, but it would have been my practice to do that. But it would not have been my practice to record any detail of notes or conversations that were held at those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Doyle. Would it be possible for you to provide this photograph and this diary to the Court, to the Tribunal? Of course once you've unpacked in New York.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The diary that is in my household effects on the way to New York is the diary of 1991 covering this -- covering the meeting I had with General Strugar, the extract of the diary for which you have in front of you. The 1992 diary and the photograph are somewhere in my files which are in my attic in my home in Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you then do us a favour and obtain this from your attic, provide this for the Court? Because on this black and white copy of the photograph, some things are barely discernible, and in the view of the Defence, they are of greater relevance to us. First of all, the first thing we would be interested in is to check where this photograph was taken, because you say that you had two meetings with General Strugar. Also, you said that the photograph was a colour photograph. The Prosecution provided us with a very poor photocopy of this photograph, although they have sophisticated technology for scanning and copying photographs. So it is quite unclear why this copy was made in such a way when we already had the opportunity of receiving colour photographs here before that were dealt with in a completely different manner. Are you prepared to provide this photograph for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, may I just say that there is absolutely no doubt that that photograph was taken on the 6th of December in the location where I met with General Strugar. There is no -- I can assure this Court there is no way that that photograph was taken on any other time but on the 6th of December. In relation to the photograph itself, the only way I can get that photograph is to physically go to my home and look for it, because I don't know exactly where it is. It is somewhere in my files. They are in my attic, and I presume it is up to the -- Your Honour to decide whether that should be done or not. It's not a question of me asking someone to get the photograph, because they're actually in an attic which contains so many files. So it would be very difficult for me to ask somebody to get the photograph. To get it, I would actually have to look for it. I wanted to bring the photograph with me when I was going to the States, but I actually couldn't find it. Now, I assume it is someplace in my files at home, because I had it before, and it is up to Your Honour if you wish that to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, I see you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like to just remind the Chamber, and I'd have to search the record on the laptop to find the passage, but General Strugar acknowledged recognising himself in photo. So the question is somewhat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's acknowledged, but not, it seems, when the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I don't know that it would lend its -- offer anything major, and I think that if the Chamber is satisfied with the explanation of, I think it's a burden we would not normally impose, and if there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The burden would appear to require the witness to travel to Ireland, which would not be, I would understand, his normal travel now as he is now living in New York.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At any time, Mr. Rodic, has the Defence called for the photograph, the original, at any earlier stage in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have not, Your Honour, because during this examination, many questions surfaced, many issues relevant to the defence, so this would be highly important to us. We would need to take a look at the back of this photograph and ascertain in this way, possibly, where the picture was taken. Also, the witness's diary would be of assistance to us if in it it is stated that he had yet another meeting with General Strugar in February 1992 in Bileca, the way he had put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that diary called for at an earlier time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this came up during the cross-examination. Beforehand, we indeed did not ask for it, but this necessity just arose now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rodic. Now, do I take it that is the end of your cross-examination? We will have the morning break now for 20 minutes and resume, and we'll give some consideration to your submission during the break. I see before we go Ms. Somers has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I wanted to inform the Chamber that my colleague Ms. McCreath indicates that those were provided 24 of September 2003 and there's been no record request at all since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers -- oh, I thought you were on your feet for a reason. I would inquire first whether the correction note, D22, is now available.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Dated the 3rd of February, 2004. Now, I must ask you to come to your feet, Ms. Somers, and the reason for that is to ask whether the quality of the photograph with which we have been provided is the best quality that is presently available to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'll just check with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: An inquiry can be made, Your Honours, of the evidence unit to see if the copy which it possesses has any better clarity. As has been explained by the witness, the original is not with the OTP. There is a possibility that there is a better copy available, and with that we could inquire -- of that we could inquire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate, Ms. Somers, that our view as a Chamber is that in view of the significance which the Prosecution places on the photograph, as we understand your case, for our purposes, the photograph is not of good quality, and we can certainly -- sorry, I don't mean the photograph, I mean the copy of it that has been provided. And we can well understand that the Defence may have further forensic purposes which would be assisted by a better quality. Ideally the original, but certainly a better quality than the quite poor reproduction presently available to us. So that our position is that we would put to the Prosecution that if it wishes the Chamber to rely upon this photograph, we would ask that appropriate steps be taken either to provide both the Defence and the Chamber with a reasonable quality copy or that whatever steps are necessary be taken to obtain the original of the photograph. We put it in that two-stage way in the hope that it will avoid the necessity for the witness to return to Ireland, something that will incur a cost of time and money and may be inconvenient, but you will appreciate that if you look at the quality of that which is presently before us, that it really is something that ought to be improved upon. May we leave it on that basis with you for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Whichever way it -- it turns out, if there is a better copy or if at some point the witness -- some point during the course of the trial, of course, the witness is in a position to assist with getting the original, and that will depend on his circumstances. I just want to make sure I understand quickly. It is not necessary that in either eventuality the witness return himself but it can be -- if found, can be transmitted, or if available, the witness is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We assume that if the original is produced, it will be able to be accepted by the Defence without the need for the witness to attend further. And can we indicate that we have also apprehended from what the witness has said that even if he does return to Ireland, there is a possibility that he may not be able to put his hands upon the photograph, but if that should be the case, we will in due course have to weigh for ourselves what weight and reliance we can place upon it as an exhibit in its present form. Well, thank you for that, Ms. Somers. And, Mr. Rodic, you will understand that we have put in place measures now to obtain, if possible, a better quality of the photograph which, if it is available, should assist you in your consideration for Defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understood what you have said with respect to the photograph, and I thank you for that. Now, may I ask whether you have made any decisions regarding the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The diary we see of a different significance. If it is the case that the witness must and does return to Ireland in search of the photograph, we would ask that his search extend to include the diary for 1992, but if it is possible to provide a satisfactory copy of the photograph without the witness having to return to Ireland, we would not separately suggest that the diary would justify his being required to return to Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Somers, your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Just briefly. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, you discussed a more -- I believe a more formal visit or a second visit -- excuse me, a second time you personally saw General Strugar in February of 1992. Did -- could you indicate the nature of that meeting and whether it was as informal as the first contact.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting with General Strugar in February 1992 was part of an itinerary that I had submitted in advance when I was informed that the head of the monitor mission wished to pay a formal visit to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And who was the head of the monitor mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the monitor mission at the time was Ambassador Salgueiro from Portugal, and he came to Bosnia with most of his senior officials; the deputy head who was a general from Portugal, the head of his political affairs, his official spokesperson, et cetera. And the meeting that was held with General Strugar was part of an itinerary which included meetings with the president, the leader of the Bosnian Serbs, the commander of the federal forces in Sarajevo, and it was on my suggestion that we include a visit down to the area of Bileca to meet with General Strugar. I accompanied the ambassador on that meeting. It had a convoy of about four cars. It included members of the Presidency. So that I was in the company of the ambassador purely because I was his representative, as it were, for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not take part in any of the formal discussions myself, even though I was part of the delegation. We were formally met by the general and his staff, treated very courteously, and there were exchanges of views and positions placed. And then, as far as I recall, the general treated us to -- to a meal. So what I would say here is that the visit was far more formal than the visit I had had in December with General Strugar which I had initiated for my own benefit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And in the course of -- or preparatory to the visit, perhaps even in the course of it, the monitors from your area of responsibility prepared a briefing on the visit of the head of mission?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My understanding was that -- the practice was that the monitor mission in Bosnia would prepare a general briefing for the benefit of the visiting dignitaries on the up-to-date events that were taking place and the personalities that they might meet with.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this briefing would be in a report or written form?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be in the form of a submission made for his consideration. They took different -- they took different formats. On one such occasion that somebody came, I would have made out suggested questions. I don't think I did it on this occasion, but we would have put a paragraph on the various -- to indicate to the head of the mission and his staff who were the major players and what the general situation was in the country.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And this type of preparation is in contrast to the type of, shall we say, preparation or maybe even lack thereof that characterised your visit to General Strugar on December 6, 1991? How would you describe the differences?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference was that I was on more or less an introductory visit when I went to Mostar on that occasion. So it was rather informal and there was no notes made out in advance, nor were there any written briefings, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would ask if the usher would be kind enough, please, to distribute a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see in front of you a document? Do you recognise it or are familiar with its contents?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This document, labelled "EC Monitor Mission Regional Centre Sarajevo Brief on the Visit of HOM," Head of Mission, if you could turn, please, to pages 0034 at the top, 00340085 and 0086. Your screen also has it if it's easier for you but I'm not sure whether it's large enough for -- okay. There's a section under paragraph 5 which discusses JNA, and do you see a mention, a bit of a briefing on General Strugar, and then at the bottom: "The following are currently the major corps units and commanders in BH." And then if you turn the page to 0086 -- I have to apologise to the Chamber and to all reading the document, the copy quality is not brilliant, but the second -- it says "Military district, military district." It says, "4th Military District, Trebinje." Is it clear? Perhaps a little bit clearer. Now, this lays out, does it not, the names of some of the key players, as you were informed, in that area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Now, if this is how the formation with the number of the military district were transmitted to you by your staff, whether correctly or incorrectly, would that be the reference you'd be making to go it? In other words, if it says 4th Military District --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. And would it make any deference to you whether or not it was 4th Military District or some other appellation? Were you satisfied that you had at least, irrespective of that or other factors, you had the players in order? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would have been -- I would have deemed it more important to have the names of the players and the location as opposed to the actual -- what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And if some of the players were listed perhaps with their names if at that stage even their titles were not necessarily correct, would you assume that they were still sufficiently important to be listed here?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'd ask to move into evidence, please, this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P49.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Colonel Doyle, I'd like to ask you if you can just help me identify some of the following names that appear -- well, some of the following names.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Izetbegovic, and please, what republic it applies to.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a member of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Djurdjevac, General? Just the basic description. Where is the focus? What republic is it focused on, what cities, if possible?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander of a JNA force in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Ah --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just say that when I arrived there first, the JNA force was increased in Sarajevo so they took in a higher ranking general who was General Kukanjac under whose command Djurdjevac would have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Ganic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ganic is a member of the Presidency. His first name is Ejub, and he is a Bosnian, as he referred to himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nikola Koljevic was a member of the Crisis Committee of the Serb SDS party and was a deputy to Radovan Karadzic who was the leader of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Where -- where would most of the activity, if you are in a position to indicate, where would most of the activity for purposes of your interview with the OTP in 1995 be focused? What was the thrust of it? What was the purpose of this actual interview? Where was the accent?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should mention here that for the second six months of my tour of duty I was the personal representative to the chairman of the International Peace Conference, Lord Peter Carrington, and as such I was based in Sarajevo. That part of my duties were involved in following mainly the political leaders in Sarajevo itself. So for the year that I would have spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would say that 85 to 90 per cent of my activities were based in and around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, can I ask for some assistance for the Tribunal, given the quality of the document which is now Exhibit P49. On the page which is 03340086 --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- do we take it that the top line commences with the number of a military district? Is it clear on any copy what that number is?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I had been given information, Your Honour, that a clearer copy showed 4th, and I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. I'm thinking of the first line --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Oh, the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I can try to get again the clearer copy that I had looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: And would be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then there is the next underlined passage, which is another military district, and General Strugar is shown as the commander, and you put to the witness that was 4th, and I think that's been accepted, but if that can be clarified. Then there is a naval group shown and Admiral Jokic's name appears against that group. Can that number of that naval group be identified?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It can and should, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as my learned colleague in her redirect introduced this document as an exhibit, I have an objection to make. In addition to what you yourself noted and observed, I would like to say something and a few extra questions, with the Court's indulgence. I think it would be important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can make your --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to the documents, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You can make your points, Mr. Rodic, but whether further questions will be allowed we'll look at separately. Firstly your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to join in what you yourself observed with respect to the page 003340086, where we can't see clearly the numbers, and we assume that they refer to military districts. I should like to draw the Court's attention, and of course to express our doubts as the Defence team with respect to this page, 086 are the last three digits of the page number. And I'd like to say that on the previous page, 03340085, 085 being the last three digits, in the last paragraph which explains the JNA, it is point 5 relating to the JNA, when describing the cause and the commanders that are listed, and generals, so in that written section, there is not a single word mentioning the 4th Military District. The 4th Military District is not mentioned anywhere. So that the Defence does not know whether this particular page 0334086 is a component part of the whole document. So apart from it being illegible, a poor copy, because previously in the written part no mention is made of the 4th Military District which allegedly was taken note of in the tabular presentation on the page of which the last digits are 086. So once we receive a legible document, a clear copy, then I should like to be allowed to state my views on it. And I would like to say something with respect to cross-examination, where the witness during cross-examination and during the examination-in-chief denied certain facts which appear in this particular report. So I would like to ask a few questions in that regard, and I should like to hear the Court's ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, I'm not inclined to allow you to re-examine on the document, but I propose myself to put some questions to the witness at this point, and they may cover some of the territory that you were concerned about, and any submissions you might have about the quality of the document can be put in due course, if it's relevant to your case, at the conclusion of your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel, at the foot -- you have the document in front of you, do you?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will try and correct that. The page which ends 085 and over to 086 are the area of interest. In paragraph on 085 which is numbered 5, near the bottom you speak of, in the middle of the big paragraph there, a 3rd Corps and then a 2nd Corps which was deployed in Trebinje from Titograd. You then refer to a corps group being currently under the command of General Strugar. To what were you then referring by the words "corps group"? Can you help with us that?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the corps group I would have in mind is the combination of the corps that are enumerated there, that when they were put together they became a corps group under the command of General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When you used the term "corps group," were you using that as an established, organised unit of the JNA or in some other --

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it was -- it was my -- it was the wording I used for a certain amount of corps being brought together. In the normal military parlance, if you put three corps together, it becomes a military division. There were no divisions mentioned in the JNA; they became groups. And therefore, I put this collective title as a corps group. To somebody else it may have been an Operational Group, but what it was was a group of corps units joined together to become a higher level, which, as I have said before, in most armies would be termed a division, but divisions were not used in that context, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You then, on the last two lines of that page, say: "The following are currently the major corps units and commanders in, abbreviated, Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then over the page, two military districts, the second perhaps including a naval group, are identified. Now, what was your reference to a military district, each of these two military districts intended to convey?

utterances.speaker: COLM DOYLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the military district would have been the location, the general location where these units were deployed.
